methods.label: Compare the cheapest orders in later tiers
methods.explanation:
Within each price tier, buying more books increases the cost. Thus any saving must come from entering a later tier, whose cheapest order is the smallest order in that tier.

For \(1\le n\le24\), the cheapest orders in the later tiers cost
\[
C(25)=275,\qquad C(49)=490.
\]
Since \(275<490\), a larger order is cheaper exactly when
\[
12n>275,
\qquad n>22\frac{11}{12}.
\]
Within this tier, the qualifying integers are \(23\) and \(24\).

For \(25\le n\le48\), the cheapest order in the final tier is \(49\) books. It is cheaper exactly when
\[
11n>490,
\qquad n>44\frac6{11}.
\]
This gives \(n=45,46,47,48\).

For \(n\ge49\), every larger order costs more because the cost is \(10n\). These three cases cover all positive integer orders without overlap, so the number of qualifying values is \(2+4=\boxed{6}\), choice \(\mathrm D\).
